What about a gas tax? No thanks, King says
While the government looks for support for its gas reservation scheme, one thing is for certain: it's not entertaining a push for a tax on exports.
The idea has been pushed by independent David Pocock and the Greens.
Resources Minister Madeleine King says her focus is on making gas more affordable and insists windfall taxes would only drive industry away from Australia.
"I'm not aware of any policy where you put a tax of that magnitude on a product that would make it more affordable to everyday Australians," she told Nine.

"It's up to every single senator to decide whether they want to vote for lower prices for gas, for more supply, for gas for Australians because that's what a vote in support of this legislation will deliver."
Earlier, Pocock told Nine the scheme as it currently stands was "pretty good".

"I'm concerned it's going to get watered down in the Senate by the Coalition but I think it's a good start. But I'm going to continue to push for a fair return for all Australians … for future generations of Australians on a resource that once it's sold, is gone."
Key Event
Coalition 'faces a choice' on gas reservation scheme: King
Resources Minister Madeleine King is still in negotiations with the Coalition as she tries to get the government's gas reservation scheme over the line.
King says senators are going to "face a choice" over the scheme but is reluctant to pre-empt whether she can win over the opposition.
The Coalition are opposed to the inclusion of Western Australia in the scheme (it has its own already set up) and has concerns about a mechanism to deliberately oversupply the domestic market.
But King tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast that her home state can't be carved out completely.

"We do have a constitution and WA is part of our federation, is part of our Commonwealth ... so having Western Australia be part of the scheme is a matter of them being part of the Commonwealth and to make the scheme robust," she says.
King on signing of joint statement calling for Israel to allow aid into Gaza
Australia signed a joint statement along with Canada, Italy and the UK calling on Israel to open crossings and allow immediate and unimpeded humanitarian access into Gaza.
So what prompted the government to sign up to the statement released today?
Resources Minister Madeleine King tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast the statement has worked on for some time.

"I'm not part of the negotiations myself but sometimes, and I know this can be difficult, but it does take time or nations to be able to work together to get the right outcome that is enduring in terms of opening these crossings," she says.
"My understanding is that time is now here and that is why we've been able to sign that agreement."
Key Event
Hume's reservations with gas scheme
Liberal deputy Jane Hume has insisted the Coalition continues to negotiate in "good faith" over a proposed gas reservation scheme.
The legislation setting up the scheme, which would require Australia's biggest exporters to set aside 20 per cent of their supply for the domestic market, is set to before the Senate this week.
But the government has yet to win over the Coalition to pass the bill. Hume says she wants to see a gas reservation but has … reservations (see what I did there).

"There are changes that need to be made. Things like West Australia should be carved out. It's an east coast gas problem that we have and there should be a specific east coast solution," she told News24."Most importantly, we do not want to do anything that would deter future investment in gas and Australia."

"There are changes that need to be made. Things like West Australia should be carved out. It's an east coast gas problem that we have and there should be a specific east coast solution," she told News24.
"Most importantly, we do not want to do anything that would deter future investment in gas and Australia."
It comes as unions and industry groups penned an open letter to the parliament, calling on it to pass the scheme.
Key Event
Australia, Canada, Italy and UK urge Israel to allow aid into Gaza
Australia has joined Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom to call for Israel to allow unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza.
In a statement, the foreign ministers said the situation on the ground in Gaza was dire.
"The recent floods have brought further suffering — and this was only the first storm of the winter," they said.
"People in Gaza desperately need shelter and humanitarian assistance.
"Yet 150,000 tents and other vital supplies are being held at the border and prevented from entering Gaza."
The group, which includes Foreign Minister Penny Wong, urged the Israel government to "stop the delays now and allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza".
"The crossings must be opened and the tents allowed in."
Albanese to meet Philippines counterpart as leaders gather for ASEAN summit
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is expected to meet Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr in Manila today, with tensions in the South China Sea expected to feature in their discussions.
The meeting follows the signing of a new defence cooperation agreement between the two countries on Sunday, expanding maritime surveillance, information sharing and military training.
Albanese will also co-chair talks with South-East Asian leaders at the ASEAN-Australia summit, where the economic fallout from wars in the Middle East and Ukraine will be a major focus.
Rising energy prices have put pressure on governments across the region, with leaders looking at ways to reduce their reliance on overseas supplies.
Trade, regional security and efforts to prevent further conflict are also on the agenda, alongside plans for a regional agreement covering the digital economy and artificial intelligence.
Albanese raises detained Australian’s case with Vietnamese PM
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has raised the case of Australian man Hiep Tran, who is detained in Vietnam, during talks with the country's new prime minister.
Albanese met Le Minh Hung on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit in Manila on Sunday, congratulating him on his appointment during their first meeting.
The leaders discussed regional security and strengthening economic ties, including cooperation under the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade agreement.
Key Event
Unions, industry join forces to call for passage of gas reservation scheme
Legislation establishing the reservation is due to go before the Senate this week. But the government still needs support from either the Coalition or the greens to get the bill over the line.
The scheme would require Australia's biggest exporters to set aside up to 20 per cent of their product for the domestic market to create a modest oversupply and put downward pressure on prices.

A collection of industry group and union leaders have today released an open letter calling on the Senate to pass the legislation. Among them is Manufacturing Australia chief Ben Eade who says the scheme is in the national interest.
Other signatories include the bosses of the Australian Workers Union and the Australian Industry Group.

Hello friends. Welcome to our politics live blog. I'm Courtney Gould from the ABC's Parliament House team, here to guide you through the day.
If you can believe it, there are only two more sitting weeks left in the parliamentary year. Today marks the start of a Senate-only week, before both Houses return next week.

The government is hoping it can get the Coalition over the line to support its gas reservation scheme through the Senate this week. Other bills on the to-do list include: digital duty of care and changes to discretionary trusts and the private health insurance rebate.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is in Manila for the ASEAN leaders' summit. More on that shortly from our friend on the ground, Clare Armstrong.
